summary: InstructGPT fine-tunes GPT-3 in three steps: supervised learning on labeler demonstrations, a reward model trained on labeler rankings, and PPO against that reward model, with a pretraining-mix variant (PPO-ptx) to reduce regressions. Labelers prefer the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3. Truthfulness improves and toxicity falls when the model is prompted to be respectful, but bias does not improve. Alignment is to an aggregate of about 40 contracted labelers and researchers, not to individual users. The model is single-turn, learns no interaction policy, and does not adapt over time. The authors discuss group-conditioned preferences only as future work. It is useful as the outcome-averaged baseline for USIL.
closest_overlap: InstructGPT is the canonical outcome_averaged baseline for USIL. Its labelers' demonstrations, rankings and pairwise comparisons are the same kinds of user evidence USIL uses, but pooled into one reward model. The Discussion section acknowledges that one cannot align to everyone at once and proposes group-conditioned models as future work [personalization].
remaining_question: Could the same SFT/RM/PPO pipeline learn per-user reward models or interaction policies, for example when to ask, confirm, or refuse, from a few of one user's own edits and approvals, given that labelers here are not the users who wrote the prompts [user_evidence]? How would that be evaluated beyond averaged labeler win rates?

summary: VPL personalizes RLHF by treating each user's preferences as a latent variable. A variational encoder infers a user latent z from a handful of that user's preference-pair annotations. A latent-conditioned BTL reward model and policies then adapt to the user without further training. The paper adds likelihood-based reward scaling (VPL-SPO) and active query selection that picks informative pairs, roughly halving the queries needed in simulated control. VPL beats BTL and DPL baselines on simulated control tasks and LLM reward modeling (e.g. 74.75 vs 49.84 on UF-P-2) and matches BTL on unimodal data. Users are simulated, preferences are static, and transfer is not evaluated. It is a strong outcome_individual predecessor.
closest_overlap: VPL infers a user-specific latent z from a few of the user's own preference annotations, which acts as z_u = g(h) in USIL. It conditions a reward model and policy on z at test time without retraining. Its mutual-information active querying is an explicit per-user elicitation decision, so it overlaps with P1, P2 and the asking part of P3.
remaining_question: Can VPL's latent-user inference and active querying be extended from static, simulated preferences over outputs to real users' procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) that drift across sessions? That would need real-user data and evaluation of transfer to new tasks or users.

summary: FSPO reframes LLM personalization as meta-learning over users: a single Llama 3.2 3B model, fine-tuned with IPO/DPO-style objectives, conditions on a user's few labeled preference pairs to infer a personalized reward and generate tailored answers. User description rationalization (RAT) and a synthetic pipeline of over 1M preferences, designed to be diverse and self-consistent, enable transfer from synthetic personas to real users. It reaches about 82-90% winrate on synthetic users and beats the base model (68%) and an SFT model (72%) in a preliminary 50-person human study. It also improves reward prediction on PRISM. It does not address interaction decisions or temporal adaptation.
closest_overlap: FSPO treats the individual user as the unit of learning, conditioning on few-shot user-specific preference evidence (an N-bit representation, optionally an inferred description) and showing sim2real transfer to 50 real Prolific users and held-out PRISM users. This is the outcome_individual counterpart of the USIL few-shot user adaptation and latent user-representation idea z_u=g(h).
remaining_question: Can the FSPO few-shot meta-learning recipe, with synthetic personas and RAT-style rationalization, be extended to infer procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, defer or return control) instead of response-content preferences? Would sim2real transfer still hold for interaction policies, and could it be evaluated longitudinally with drifting users?

summary: Decision-theoretic principles for when an agent should act, ask (engage in dialog), or do nothing, based on expected utility and uncertainty.

This position paper proposes five levels of agent autonomy defined by the role the user plays: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver and observer. It treats autonomy as a design choice distinct from capability and environment. It sketches autonomy certificates for governance and assisted evaluations that assign a level from the minimum user involvement needed to reach a performance threshold. A running example illustrates each level, and open questions ask when an agent should consult or seek approval. There are no experiments, learning mechanisms or user data. Personalization appears only conceptually, as user-specified approval conditions and a possible L3 training period. It is useful as a vocabulary for procedure-level autonomy that is averaged across users.
closest_overlap: Treats autonomy as a design decision about how the agent works, separate from capability. It defines levels in terms of when the agent consults, asks approval, or hands over control, which are the decisions USIL wants learned per user. L4 users specify approval conditions and L3 agents may need a training period to learn user expertise and preferences [personalization].
remaining_question: How could the autonomy level, or the consult/approve boundary within a level, be learned and adjusted per user from approvals, takeovers and corrections over time, and could assisted evaluations be extended to measure individual-level calibration rather than a single agent-level certificate?

summary: τ-bench is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in retail and airline domains. An LM simulates a human user with a task instruction, the agent has domain APIs and a policy document, and success is judged by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state. The paper introduces pass^k, the probability that all k i.i.d. trials succeed, to measure reliability. Twelve LMs are tested with function calling, ReAct and Act. The best, gpt-4o, reaches 61.2% pass^1 in retail and 35.2% in airline, with pass^8 below 25% in retail. Nothing is learned and there is no personalization or longitudinal adaptation, but it is a useful procedural evaluation baseline.
closest_overlap: The benchmark scores procedural interaction behavior (each turn the agent chooses between a tool call and a user message, gathers information, confirms before writes, refuses prohibited requests, and transfers to a human). It runs these with LM-simulated users with different identities and preferences [interaction_decisions][user_evidence]. This covers the procedure row and offers a simulator and reliability metric that USIL evaluation could build on.
remaining_question: Can τ-bench's simulated users be extended to have persistent, individually varying interaction preferences (e.g., how often they want confirmation, how much autonomy to grant) across repeated sessions, so that per-user adaptation of ask/confirm/act behavior can be measured, with pass^k used to separate real adaptation from noise?

summary: This between-subjects study (N=73) compares Traditional GUI, AI-First and Hybrid modes in an LLM-augmented REST web app built with an MCP architecture, using 16 CRUD tasks. AI assistance reduced clicks, navigations and scrolling but did not change task time. In the Hybrid condition, chat use did not differ significantly by CRUD operation, yet the by-participant intercept explained about half the variance (ICC=.50), so delegation varies more across users than tasks. No model is trained and nothing is personalized; adaptive designs are only suggested. The sample is homogeneous, with a single app and model and one fixed task order, so transfer is untested.
closest_overlap: The Hybrid condition lets users choose per task between GUI manipulation and delegating to an LLM agent, and the finding that delegation varies far more across users than tasks (ICC=.50) is direct empirical motivation for treating the individual user as a unit for procedural adaptation.
remaining_question: Can a per-user delegation or autonomy policy be learned from a few logged GUI-versus-chat choices (the ICC=.50 signal) and shown to beat a population-level default for when the agent should act, ask or hand control back, and does it stay stable across applications, models and sessions?

summary: A within-subjects study of 20 AI-literate CS students used a general-purpose agent on five tasks that varied in privacy, stakes and reversibility. Trust was calibrated per task: it was lowest, and approval preference highest, for the email-sending task, where the agent acted without showing a preview. Participants often rated outputs as successful yet regretted that the agent had acted without authorization, which the authors name 'delegation regret'. They argue that irreversibility plus external visibility, not stakes alone, drives trust withdrawal, and they propose an agent management layer with user-specified autonomy levels. The study is small, uncounterbalanced and single-session, and it contains no personalization or learning.
closest_overlap: The paper shows that dissatisfaction with a general-purpose agent comes from acting beyond the user's authorization boundary, not from wrong output. It also finds that trust and approval preferences vary by task, with irreversibility and external visibility (the email-sending task T2) driving the need for confirmation. This directly motivates procedure-level evaluation and adaptive autonomy and confirmation, the core of USIL, though only at the population level [key_results][interaction_decisions].
remaining_question: Do the confirmation and autonomy preferences found here (preview and approval before irreversible, externally visible actions such as email) vary systematically across individual users? If they do, can an agent learn them per user from approvals, rejections and takeovers over repeated sessions, rather than having users set autonomy levels by action type up front? The paper reports only group-level statistics from a single fixed-order session and an unevaluated proposal [personalization][temporal_adaptation].

summary: The paper introduces modeling human intervention in collaborative web agents. COWCORPUS holds 400 real-user trajectories (20 users, 20 tasks each) with over 4,200 interleaved human and agent actions. K-means clustering yields four interaction styles: Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off and Collaborative. Fine-tuned LMMs (Gemma-27B, LLaVA-8B) predict at each step whether the user will intervene and outperform prompted closed models on Perfect Timing Score. Style-conditioned models generally do best on their own cluster, except Takeover. In a small user study (n=16), the deployed PlowPilot, which prompts only when intervention is likely, was rated 36.8% more useful than CowPilot. Personalization is at cluster level, with no cross-session adaptation or transfer shown.
closest_overlap: It is close to USIL's procedural focus: it learns when an agent should hand control to the user (ask vs. continue) from real interleaved human-agent web trajectories, and conditions the policy on interaction style (Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off, Collaborative). The style-conditioned models are an intermediate step between averaged and individual interaction policies [personalization][what_is_learned].
remaining_question: Do style-cluster models extend to per-user pi_u that adapt online from a few interventions for a new user, including the data-sparse Takeover-like users, and do they transfer to unseen tasks, sites, and users across sessions? The paper does not establish this [transfer][temporal_adaptation][limitations].

summary: The paper introduces personalized benchmarking for LLMs. Using Chatbot Arena votes from 115 users with at least 25 battles, it computes per-user ELO and Bradley-Terry rankings over 20 models and finds that they diverge from global rankings (mean Spearman 0.432 for ELO, 0.043 for BT). Users also differ in query topics and writing style. A regression on topic and style features predicts user-specific rankings better than a mean-predictor baseline that mimics an aggregate benchmark (MAE reduced by 35% for ELO and 12% for BT). It studies no interaction decisions, temporal adaptation or transfer, and the validation set is small (18 users). It is correlational.
closest_overlap: It treats the individual user as the unit of evaluation rather than the average user, showing that per-user Chatbot Arena rankings diverge from global ones (BT mean Spearman 0.043) and that topic+style features predict them better than a mean-predictor baseline. This supports USIL's critique of averaged evaluation, but only on the outcome side.
remaining_question: Can individual-level divergence be shown for procedural preferences (when users want clarification, confirmation or autonomy) rather than which LLM's response they prefer? Can per-user profiles predict such preferences for new users, over time and across tasks, beyond an 18-user held-out split of the same dataset?

summary: This paper compares four human-oversight strategies for LLM computer-use agents (Risk-Gated, Action Confirmation, Supervisory Co-Execution, Structurally Enriched) in 192 live sessions with a shared base agent and task environment. Plan-based strategies reduced the odds of problematic actions by 76%, but users blocked only 29 of 138 problematic actions that reached execution, with no reliable difference across strategies. Video coding shows that authority is often mistimed and that users check procedural correctness. The authors argue that oversight should adapt over time, but nothing is learned or personalized, and there is no transfer evaluation. It is useful as population-level evidence on procedural interaction timing.
closest_overlap: It studies the procedural side of human-agent work: when a GUI agent should hand control back through confirmation, plan approval or risk-flagged escalation, and how users delegate, inspect and intervene. It shows that these timing choices matter for safety. This is the procedure_averaged cell that USIL contrasts with per-user policies.
remaining_question: Do users differ systematically in how they delegate, inspect and intervene, and so in the right timing and granularity of control return? Could a per-user policy learned from approvals, interventions and takeovers over repeated sessions fix the mistimed authority that this paper finds under population-level strategies?

summary: Review of how trust in automation forms, evolves with experience, and governs reliance.
Learns context-sensitive individual interruption costs and deploys notifications

The Off-Switch Game is a one-shot game-theoretic analysis of why a rational agent would allow a human to switch it off. A robot that is uncertain about the human's utility, and treats the human's off-switch decision as evidence about that utility, has a positive incentive to defer. A robot with a fixed, known reward lacks this incentive unless the human is rational. For a noisily rational human, the incentive depends on a tradeoff between the robot's uncertainty and the human's suboptimality. The paper has no learning, personalization, temporal adaptation, or empirical evaluation. It is a formal foundation for deference and autonomy decisions relevant to P3.
closest_overlap: The paper formalizes when an agent should defer to a human rather than act, using uncertainty about the human's utility and treating the human's switch-off decision as evidence (Theorems 1-2, Corollary 1). This is a theoretical basis for the P3 question of when to defer or return control [interaction_decisions][key_results].
remaining_question: How can off-switch-style deference incentives be extended from a single, population-level, one-shot game to a sequential setting where the agent learns a per-user belief over each user's preferences about oversight, using that user's approvals, rejections, and takeovers over time? The authors name sequential settings and model misspecification as future work [temporal_adaptation][limitations].

summary: This ICML 2024 paper introduces Dynamic Reward MDPs (DR-MDPs) to analyze AI decision-making when a person's reward function changes over time and can be influenced by the AI. It shows that common alignment objectives, such as real-time reward and initial reward, can incentivize undesirable influence, lock-in, or poor real-time reward, and that changing the horizon cannot reliably remove these incentives. Comparing 8 notions of alignment on toy examples, it finds each either permits undesirable influence or is overly risk-averse, with the proposed ParetoUD often reducing to inaction. The work is purely theoretical: reward functions and their dynamics are assumed known, with no user data or learning.
closest_overlap: DR-MDPs formalize preferences that change over time and respond to the AI's own actions. This is the drift-versus-influence problem USIL faces when adapting a pi_u to evolving user evidence: an agent learning from a user's reactions can shift the user it is modeling. The analysis of real-time, initial, final and natural-shift objectives and of horizon effects speaks directly to what a longitudinal per-user policy should optimize [temporal_adaptation][key_results].
remaining_question: When a per-user interaction policy (when to ask, confirm, or defer) is learned from edits and corrections, how can it be kept from steering the user's procedural preferences in undesirable ways, and could a ParetoUD-like constraint be made less conservative using estimated user-specific reward dynamics rather than a known model?

summary: The paper asks when an agent should ask users to confirm intermediate steps in long multi-step agentic tasks. A formative study identifies a confirmation-diagnosis-correction-rollback (CDCR) pattern. The authors build a decision-theoretic dynamic-programming scheduler that places checkpoints to minimize expected user time. In a 48-participant within-subjects study against confirm-at-end, the scheduler cut completion time by 13.54% and was preferred by 81%. Gains were largest for early errors and slightly negative for late errors. Parameters are population-level and fixed. Personalization and online adaptation are explicitly deferred to future work, and time is the only cost modeled.
closest_overlap: It directly addresses when an agent should ask for confirmation versus proceed autonomously in long-horizon tasks, which is the P3 decision USIL wants to personalize. It frames confirmation as a time-minimizing decision-theoretic schedule and shows an averaged-population version beating confirm-at-end by 13.54% with 81% preference [key_results][interaction_decisions]. It is a clean procedure_averaged baseline.
remaining_question: Can the per-user timing and accuracy-belief parameters (confirmation time, diagnosis time, trust in the agent) be learned online from sparse real interaction history, and does a per-user checkpoint schedule beat this population-level one in longitudinal deployment, beyond time cost?

summary: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic, inference-time Value of Information framework for LLM agents deciding whether to ask a clarifying question or act on an underspecified request. The LLM estimates a belief over latent user intent, simulates the answers to candidate questions, and asks only when expected utility gain exceeds the communication cost. It needs no threshold tuning. Across 20 Questions, flight preference, and ambiguous WebShop, with GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash, VoI matches or beats tuned baselines in 18 of 20 conditions, but trails at higher costs. Users are simulated, and adaptation is limited to a single dialogue. It is a strong population-level procedural baseline for USIL.
closest_overlap: The VoI clarify-or-commit policy is a principled, tuning-free instantiation of the ask-versus-act decision (P3) that USIL wants to make user-specific. The flight-preference task infers a latent per-user reward function from five rounds of choice history plus clarifying questions [personalization], so it does touch on per-user inference within a dialogue.
remaining_question: Can the VoI communication cost c and the stakes or utility scale be learned per user, for example from interruptions, answer latency or skipped questions, so the ask/commit threshold becomes user-specific and persists across sessions with real users rather than simulated ones?

summary: Foundational learning interface agents; slightly before the requested 1995 boundary

This 2004 IJHCS paper reports a questionnaire survey of 42 users with varying expertise on interface agents, using the authors' agents or MS Office assistants. It examines which user–agent interaction issues need personalization in mixed-initiative settings: assistant type, allowed assistance actions, interruptions, error tolerance, feedback and autonomy. Preferences are heterogeneous. Only 12% want a collaborative agent, 49% allow suggestions but not autonomous action, and tolerance for errors and willingness to give feedback decline over time. The authors derive eight lessons and propose a user interaction profile of situation–action pairs with probabilities. No system is built, learned or evaluated; the profiling algorithms are future work.
closest_overlap: The paper argues that mixed-initiative interaction issues (assistant type, allowed autonomy, interruption tolerance, error tolerance, feedback willingness) vary across users and need per-user profiles. It proposes a profile of situation–agent-action pairs with probabilities [what_is_learned][personalization]. This is an early, motivational form of USIL's pi_u, aimed at procedural rather than outcome personalization.
remaining_question: Can per-user interaction profiles of situation–action probabilities, with confidence thresholds for autonomy and interruption, be learned from sparse behavioural traces (accept/reject, takeover, ignored suggestions) rather than self-reports? Would they track the drift in error tolerance and feedback willingness seen over time, and outperform population-level or expertise-group defaults?

summary: Direct statement to learn how to interact with each user; assistance timing/type
Interface agents that learn when and how to interrupt or assist each user without being intrusive.

This paper proposes a human-robot mutual adaptation formalism for shared autonomy. A bounded-memory model of human adaptability (BAM) is embedded in a MOMDP with a disagreement penalty. The robot maintains a belief over each user's goal and adaptability α and decides whether to guide the user toward an optimal goal or comply with their preference. In a 51-participant table-clearing study, the mutual-adaptation robot raised team performance over one-way adaptation (following the user) while keeping trust higher than a no-adaptation baseline. Adaptation is within-task only, α is fixed, the model is hand-specified, and transfer is untested.
closest_overlap: The robot maintains a per-user belief over adaptability α and uses it to choose between steering the user toward a better goal and deferring to the user's preference. This is a per-user autonomy/deference policy [personalization][interaction_decisions]. It is close to USIL's pi_u over act and defer decisions, but it is inferred within a single task rather than learned across sessions.
remaining_question: Can a per-user adaptability or compliance parameter like α be learned across sessions, allowed to drift over time, and transferred to new tasks, rather than fixed within one table-clearing task and hand-specified in the model?

summary: PRELUDE/CIPHER studies how a frozen LLM agent can learn from user edits to its outputs. The LLM infers a natural-language description of the user's latent preference from each (output, edit) pair. At test time, descriptions from the k most similar past contexts are aggregated into the prompt, so no fine-tuning is needed. In GPT-4 simulated-user summarization and email-writing environments, CIPHER cuts cumulative edit cost by 31% and 73% against baselines and has the best preference accuracy. A small human study supports this. It does not cover interaction decisions, drift, or transfer, and a gap to the oracle remains.
closest_overlap: CIPHER learns an individual user's latent, context-dependent preference from implicit feedback (edits) via retrieval over interaction history, with no fine-tuning. It is close to USIL's user-specific evidence and h_t^u memory, and an edit-triggered LPI skip (δ threshold) is the nearest thing to an adaptive interaction choice. The learned object is output style, not interaction behavior.
remaining_question: Can edit-derived preference descriptions be extended to procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) and be tested with real, evolving users and cross-task transfer, rather than a GPT-4 simulated user with fixed per-source preferences?

summary: The paper presents General User Models (GUMs): per-user collections of natural-language, confidence-weighted propositions learned from unstructured computer observations (screenshots, notifications, emails) by prompting off-the-shelf LLMs and VLMs. A Propose, Retrieve, Revise, Audit pipeline updates propositions over time with decay scores. Applications query the GUM, including Gumbo, a proactive assistant that uses an expected-utility rule and rate limiting to decide when to interrupt. An email study (N=18) shows retrieval and revision improve win rate and calibration; a five-day Gumbo deployment (N=5) gives 0.79 accuracy, though only 25% of suggestions were rated strong or excellent. Cross-application transfer is claimed but not systematically tested.
closest_overlap: Each user builds their own GUM from interaction evidence, which persists and is revised over time, and Gumbo's expected-utility interruption rule with feedback fed back into the GUM touches on per-user autonomy and interruption decisions [personalization][interaction_decisions][temporal_adaptation]. This is close to USIL's z_u = g(h) and pi_u idea, but the GUM mainly models what the user knows, believes and prefers (outcome-individual) and does not learn an interaction policy.
remaining_question: Can GUM-style propositions be extended to capture procedural preferences (when this user wants to be asked, interrupted, or confirmed, or to take over), with the interruption utility and thresholds learned per user from thumbs and text feedback and tested across tasks and users, rather than set from elicited costs and a fixed 1-per-minute limit?

summary: CollabLLM trains LLMs to be active collaborators in multiturn dialogue. It estimates Multiturn-aware Rewards by simulating future turns with an LLM user simulator, then fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B with SFT, DPO, or PPO. The resulting policy asks clarifying questions and makes suggestions when requests are ambiguous. In simulation it improves task performance by 18.5%, interactivity by 46.3%, and efficiency by 13.3%. A 201-person user study shows 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less time spent. Zero-shot transfer to Abg-CoQA shows more clarification. It does no per-user personalization or cross-session adaptation, and the authors list personalization as future work.
closest_overlap: CollabLLM learns an interaction policy for when to ask clarifying questions, offer suggestions, or answer directly, by optimizing multiturn-aware rewards with simulated users. It is a population-level (procedure_averaged) version of what USIL wants per user, and it shows that forward-looking RL can shift asking behavior (~50% clarification on ambiguous inputs zero-shot) [interaction_decisions][transfer].
remaining_question: Can Multiturn-aware Rewards be conditioned on a user-specific history h_u, with simulators that vary in how often they want to be asked or how much autonomy they grant, so that the clarify/suggest/act policy adapts per user over sessions and not just within a conversation? Does that still hold when real users differ from the simulators?

summary: The paper proposes offline RL to learn AI-assistance policies in AI-assisted decision-making that optimize human-centric objectives, namely immediate accuracy and learning. A tabular Q-learning policy over a 64-state space (Need for Cognition, concept, AI correctness, knowledge) selects among four assistance types. Policies are learned from data on 142 participants making exercise-prescription decisions, then tested in two new studies. Accuracy-optimized policies beat baselines for both NFC groups, sometimes achieving complementarity. Learning-optimized policies helped only low-NFC users in Experiment 1 and showed no significant effect in Experiment 2. Personalization is group-level, with a single task and crowd participants, and no transfer is tested.
closest_overlap: It learns an adaptive policy over how AI assistance is delivered (explanation, recommendation, withholding) with offline RL, conditioned on a user trait (Need for Cognition) and on running knowledge, and it optimizes human-centric objectives such as learning instead of accuracy only. This is close to USIL's idea of a user-conditioned interaction policy, but conditioning is on two NFC groups, not individual histories.
remaining_question: Can offline RL policies of this type be conditioned on individual interaction history (edits, overrides, reliance patterns) rather than a median-split NFC group, and still deliver gains in accuracy and learning across sessions, tasks, and expert users, given that learning gains were weak and non-replicated in Experiment 2?

summary: TAACo personalizes a household robot's manner of assistance (do now, do later, remind, or no action) from sparse verbal feedback. GPT-4 scores abstract concepts for each task, and a per-user transformer is trained on these scores plus state variables, with attention aligned to user explanations. In interviews with five older adults (173 tasks), TAACo reached 0.71 prediction accuracy with 40 samples and 0.74 explanation accuracy, beating few-shot GPT-4 and a rule-based baseline. It generalizes to held-out tasks within each user. It does not study temporal drift, cross-user transfer, or asking decisions, and the sample is small.
closest_overlap: It learns per-user procedural preferences, meaning whether the robot acts now, acts later, reminds, or does nothing, from sparse verbal feedback from five older adults. It does so with person-specific models and transfers to held-out tasks. This is close to the procedure_individual cell, using abstract concepts as a user representation z_u.
remaining_question: Can concept-based per-user adaptation preferences be learned online from implicit evidence (takeovers, corrections) and updated as preferences drift over sessions? Can they extend to decisions about when to ask or confirm, and can they transfer across users or to new contexts rather than only new tasks within one user's data?

summary: The paper proposes automating data-access permissions for AI agents with an assistant that learns each user's allow/deny preferences. A vignette study with 205 Prolific participants identifies the factors that shape permission decisions. A hybrid predictor combines o3-mini in-context learning on the user's own history and demographics with LightGCN collaborative filtering over other users. It reaches 85.1% accuracy overall and 94.4% at 25.9% coverage when only high-confidence predictions are automated and uncertain ones are deferred to the user. Accuracy improves with more history, but high-variance users are hard to predict. It is a proof of concept with no temporal evaluation and no external baselines.
closest_overlap: The paper learns an individual user's procedural preference, namely whether to permit data access without asking, from that user's decision history, and routes low-confidence cases back to the user. This is close to a user-conditioned pi_u over act versus defer or ask, with per-user analysis of predictability [personalization][interaction_decisions].
remaining_question: Do per-user permission-delegation preferences remain stable and transfer across sessions, tasks and real agent deployments, and can the confidence-based defer rule be learned per user, with drift handled, rather than set by a global threshold on vignette data?

summary: PrefIx is a configurable simulation environment for evaluating how LLM agents interact, not just what they accomplish. Its Interaction-as-a-Tool paradigm casts interaction behaviors (confirmation, narration, clarification, error handling) as structured tool calls. A taxonomy of 14 preference attributes (31 settings) drives a preference-guided user simulator that expresses preferences only implicitly. Seven UX dimensions and preference alignment are scored by a validated multi-LLM-judge ensemble. Prompting four LLMs to infer preferences from a sample history improved UX by 7.6% and alignment by 18.5% on average, while generally preserving tool accuracy. Nothing is trained, and long-term adaptation, transfer and real users are not tested.
closest_overlap: PrefIx treats procedural interaction preferences (confirmation, transparency, pacing, error handling) as the thing to infer and adapt to. It evaluates this through interaction tool calls that map onto USIL's ask/confirm/explain/defer decisions, with a P vs No_P comparison and preference-alignment scoring against ground-truth trajectories [personalization][interaction_decisions][key_results]. It is the closest benchmark-level instantiation of the procedure_individual cell.
remaining_question: PrefIx uses simulated users with single, fixed preference labels and a provided history. Can agents infer and update interaction preferences online from real, sparse, evolving evidence (edits, takeovers, corrections) with compound or conflicting preferences, and carry them across sessions and tasks? Long-term adaptation and transfer are untested [temporal_adaptation][transfer][limitations].

summary: The paper introduces Generative Active Task Elicitation (GATE). Instead of users writing prompts or labeling examples, a language model interviews them with open-ended questions, yes/no questions or generated edge cases for five minutes. A GPT-4 predictor conditioned on the transcript then predicts that user's labels. Across content recommendation, moral reasoning and email validation, GATE often beats user-written prompts, supervised learning and pool-based active learning, with equal or lower reported mental effort. No model is trained, the question policy is prompt-only, and adaptation is single-session. It is a close predecessor for per-user elicitation but targets output preferences, not interaction procedure.
closest_overlap: GATE elicits each user's preferences with LM-generated open-ended questions and edge cases, then conditions a predictor on that user's transcript and scores per-user agreement. This is per-user adaptation from user answers, the same evidence type USIL names. The policy chooses which question to ask, which overlaps with USIL's ask/clarify decisions.
remaining_question: GATE elicits preferences about the task output (what content to recommend, moral judgments, email validity). Can the same elicitation learn how a user wants the agent to behave (when to ask, confirm or defer), and do those elicited interaction preferences persist and transfer across sessions and tasks? The questioning policy is also the same for every user. Could it be adapted per user?

summary: The paper teaches LLMs (Llama2, Gemma, Llama3) to ask clarifying questions for ambiguous QA by labeling DPO preferences through simulated future turns. A user simulator answers the clarifying question, and the downstream answer's F1 against each interpretation's gold answer decides whether asking or answering directly is preferred. This double-turn labeling gives about 5% higher F1 than single-turn preferences. A clarify-or-direct model also learns when clarification is needed and beats a random baseline. Users are simulated from dataset annotations, interactions last at most two turns, and there is no cross-session or per-user adaptation. Transfer to other tasks is left as future work.
closest_overlap: It trains an LLM policy over ask-versus-answer decisions, using simulated users to score the future consequences of asking. This is the population-level clarification policy that USIL treats as the procedure_averaged baseline. Preference labels are kept per simulated annotator/interpretation, which loosely resembles user-conditioned evidence, but only within one conversation.
remaining_question: Could the double-turn simulated-outcome preference labeling be conditioned on a persistent user history, so that the clarify-versus-answer threshold adapts to an individual user's tolerance for questions and ambiguity-resolution habits, rather than being a single population policy trained against simulated gold-answer users?

summary: MultiSessionCollab is a benchmark for long-term collaboration in which user simulators with personas and three interaction preferences each work with an agent over 20 sessions. The agent keeps a reflective natural-language memory of user preferences, contexts and satisfying strategies, and the reflection policy is trained with GRPO using rewards from simulator behavior. Memory improves task success and reduces user effort and conversation length versus no memory, Mem0 and history baselines, and approaches an oracle. A 19-participant study corroborates the gains but shows weaker cross-domain generalization. Preferences are explicit and static, and ask/act/defer decisions are neither learned nor evaluated.
closest_overlap: Each simulated user has three assigned interaction preferences (how the agent should behave), which the agent learns across 20 sessions into a per-user memory that changes later behavior. This is close to procedure_individual learning, and the user-effort metric (preference enforcements) is a procedural evaluation beyond task success [personalization][metrics_and_baselines][temporal_adaptation].
remaining_question: MultiSessionCollab learns what a user prefers but not when to ask, confirm, act or defer, and its preferences are explicit and static. Can a user-conditioned policy learn these decisions from implicit signals such as edits and takeovers under drifting preferences, and transfer to unseen tasks or users?

summary: PAHF (Personalized Agents from Human Feedback) is a continual personalization framework in which a prompted LLM agent learns per-user natural-language preference notes in isolated external memory. It combines proactive pre-action clarification, asked when an instruction is ambiguous and memory lacks relevant information, with reactive post-action feedback that revises memory under preference drift. A four-phase protocol on new embodied-manipulation and online-shopping benchmarks uses simulated personas. PAHF beats No Memory, Pre-action Only and Post-action Only baselines in all phases, and Pre-action Only collapses after drift. Transfer is tested only within a persona, and feedback is simulated and noise-free.
closest_overlap: PAHF learns per-user memory online from live interaction. It couples pre-action clarification (an ask decision) with post-action feedback to handle drift, and it evaluates across a four-phase longitudinal protocol. This is close to USIL's user-specific history h_t^u and its evolving, sparse evidence. Its sharpest overlap is deciding whether to ask based on what memory already contains.
remaining_question: PAHF's memory stores mostly declarative content preferences and only a one-question ask/no-ask decision. It does not show whether it can learn a per-user procedural policy, such as when a given user wants to be asked, confirmed with, or left alone. Nor does it show whether that policy transfers across users or domains, or holds up with real humans and noisy feedback instead of simulated personas.

summary: The paper introduces UserVille, which turns static datasets into vague-prompt tasks with LLM user simulators holding hidden precise prompts and one of 20 interaction preferences. It also introduces PPP, a multi-objective RL method that jointly optimizes task productivity, proactivity (low user effort) and personalization (preference compliance). An agent trained on Seed-OSS-36B learns when to ask clarifying questions and how to phrase them, outperforming GPT-5 on average (+16.72), and generalizes to unseen preferences, other simulators and full SWE tasks. A 33-person user study partly confirms this but shows a sim-to-real effort gap. Personalization is preference-conditioned, not learned per user over time.
closest_overlap: PPP trains a single RL policy over ask-versus-act decisions and rewards adherence to 20 simulated users' interaction preferences (selection-only, JSON, language), so it evaluates procedural adaptation and generalization to 8 held-out preferences. This is the closest existing instance of learning how an agent interacts rather than only what it produces.
remaining_question: Can PPP-style training be extended so the agent infers an individual user's interaction preferences from sparse, noisy, evolving evidence (edits, answers, takeovers) across sessions, instead of receiving one of 20 stated preferences, and does it still work with real users given the sim-to-real gap in effort estimation?

summary: Hedwig is a CLI coding agent demo that adapts its autonomy from developer interaction traces rather than static permission settings or instruction files. Hard constraints sit alongside learned behavioral guidance. An online logistic regression over 13 action features, updated by SGD after each decision and persisted per repository, scores each proposed action into silent approval, flagged approval, or live check-in. Corrections are stored as text snippets and retrieved into prompts. A synthetic-persona evaluation against Claude Code with Auto Memory shows higher recall for a cautious persona but more false positives for a permissive one. There is no user study and no transfer evaluation, so the authors frame it as a proof of concept.
closest_overlap: Hedwig learns a per-repository, evidence-driven check-in policy from developer approvals and denials, with coefficients persisted across sessions, so it directly instantiates a user-conditioned policy for when to confirm, act, or ask. It differs from USIL in that personalization is keyed to the repository, not an individual user, and it is shown only with synthetic personas.
remaining_question: Does a per-repository check-in classifier trained on real developers' approvals transfer across repositories and tasks for the same developer, and can it separate genuine preference drift from noise, given the fixed threshold and no recency weighting?

summary: The paper identifies an access-compliance gap in coding agents: they can retrieve a user's remembered corrections and still violate them (compliance is 31.6% with no rules, 55.0% with all rules). Trace, a drop-in skill-layer pipeline, compiles chat corrections into a per-user library of atomic rules, each with an applicability check, a behavior instruction and a verifier. A lifecycle resolver maintains the library, and runtime hooks block task completion until active verifiers pass. On ClawArena and MemoryArena-derived tasks with simulated users, Trace lowers violations and user turns versus Mem0, Hindsight and ReMe-Light. OOD transfer is strong on ClawArena and weak on MemoryArena.
closest_overlap: Trace is close to procedure_individual: it turns each user's own corrections into a persistent per-user library of procedural rules that gate agent behavior in later sessions, and it measures violation and repeated corrections rather than only task success. It also shows that remembered preferences (Mem0, All Rules) are often not followed.
remaining_question: Trace enforces a fixed rule set as hard gates, so it does not learn when to ask, confirm, defer or hand back control per user. Can per-user rules be turned into a learned, calibrated interaction policy that adapts autonomy and confirmation, and that stays effective as preferences drift in an online setting with real rather than simulated users, given that the evaluation freezes the store and MemoryArena OOD violation stays near 97%?

summary: KnowU-Bench is an online Android-emulator benchmark for interactive, proactive, and personalized mobile agents, with 42 general, 86 personalized, and 64 proactive tasks. A hidden-profile LLM user simulator (gpt-4o) supplies clarification answers and consent or rejection. Agents see only timestamped behavior logs, clean or noisy, and must infer preferences or ask. In proactive tasks they choose between acting, proposing, and staying silent, and must stop after rejection. Hybrid rule and LLM-judge scoring is used. Of 11 models, Claude Sonnet 4.6 is best (60.4% SR), but hard personalized tasks peak at 44.2%. Failures are mostly poor clarification and miscalibrated intervention. No learning or temporal adaptation is studied.
closest_overlap: It evaluates procedural, user-specific behavior (asking via ask_user, proposing for confirmation, staying silent, stopping after rejection) against hidden per-role profiles in a live Android environment. This is the closest benchmark to USIL's procedure-by-individual cell [interaction_decisions][personalization].
remaining_question: KnowU-Bench uses four synthetic personas with static logs and no learning. Can agents learn a per-user interaction policy (when to ask, act, or stay silent) from accumulating corrections and rejections over sessions, and does it transfer to new tasks and apps? The benchmark does not test this [temporal_adaptation][transfer].

summary: VitaBench 2.0 is a benchmark of temporally ordered tool-use task sequences for 56 synthetic users with over 2,000 preferences, three domains (Delivery, In-store, OTA) and 66 tools. Preferences drift between tasks, and histories are fragmented and noisy. Some tasks are proactive, so the agent must ask or explore to fill in missing context. An UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface compares full context, agentic memory and RAG across about 25 LLM configurations. The best model reaches Avg@4 of about 0.5 and Pass^4 of about 0.3. Memory usually hurts, performance degrades over the sequence, and proactive scores trail personalization scores. Nothing is trained and transfer is not tested.
closest_overlap: VitaBench 2.0 is a longitudinal per-user benchmark with 56 users and 2,000+ preferences, drift events and an UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface. It is the closest existing testbed for USIL's evaluation pillar. It also measures proactive asking when context is missing, and finds proactive scores consistently below personalization scores (Claude 27.4 vs 46.0).
remaining_question: The benchmark scores whether the right item is chosen and whether missing information is requested. It does not measure per-user procedural preferences such as how often a given user wants to be asked or confirmed, or when they want to take back control. Can USIL's per-user interaction policies be evaluated on this benchmark, e.g. by adding user-specific ask/confirm tolerances to the restricted simulator, and do they transfer across the three domains?

summary: Classic debate: user-controlled direct manipulation versus autonomous interface agents that act on the user's behalf.

PERSONAMEM is a benchmark of 20 synthetic personas with over 180 multi-session user-chatbot histories (up to 1M tokens), generated with GPT-4o. Seven in-situ query types test recalling facts, tracking evolving preferences, and generalizing to new scenarios. Models choose among four candidate responses. Fifteen LLMs reach only about 50% accuracy, struggle to incorporate the user's latest state, and do poorly on new scenarios. Reasoning models show no clear advantage. RAG and Mem0 improve accuracy, with RAG usually better. The benchmark is individual-level and longitudinal, but it covers output personalization only and has no interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
closest_overlap: PERSONAMEM evaluates individual-level personalization over long, evolving multi-session histories, including a 'generalize to new scenarios' query type and memory modules (RAG, Mem0). This matches USIL's P2 and P4 on user-specific history and cross-context transfer. It is an outcome-focused counterpart: it measures whether responses reflect the user's current profile, not how the agent works.
remaining_question: Can PERSONAMEM-style persona histories and timestamped preference drift be extended with procedural signals (corrections, approvals, takeovers, ask/confirm preferences) so benchmarks can measure whether an agent learns per-user decisions about when to ask, act, or defer, beyond selecting profile-consistent responses?

summary: Co-Gym is an open framework for developing and evaluating LM agents that collaborate with humans, with dual control of task environments and non-turn-taking interaction. It supports simulated users (gpt-4o with hidden preferences) and real users (99 participants, 150 trajectories) across Travel Planning, Related Work, and Tabular Analysis. Prompted agents (autonomous, collaborative, and situational-planning) are compared on delivery, task performance, initiative entropy, and satisfaction. Collaborative agents win 66-86% against autonomous ones in the real condition. Error analysis finds failures in communication, situational awareness, and personalization. No learning occurs and adaptation stays within one session, leaving cross-session, per-user interaction learning open.
closest_overlap: It evaluates procedural aspects of collaboration (initiative balance, proactive confirmation, act/message/wait decisions, non-turn-taking coordination) with 99 real participants. Its error taxonomy names failure to adapt to individual in-session preferences (16% of real trajectories) and to carry preferences into future interactions (P.3). That is the gap USIL targets, but the paper results are averaged across users.
remaining_question: Can the Co-Gym dual-control, non-turn-taking setup be extended with longitudinal, repeated-user sessions and per-user metrics, so that an agent could learn user-specific initiative and confirmation policies, and procedural personalization could be measured separately from task outcomes?

summary: PLUS (Preference Learning Using Summarization) personalizes RLHF reward models without user IDs. A PPO-trained LLM summarizer turns each user's context, such as past conversations, into a short natural-language preference summary. A reward model conditioned on that summary predicts chosen vs. rejected responses, and the two are trained jointly. PLUS beats Bradley-Terry-Luce reward models by 11–77% on Pets and UltraFeedback and stays above 90% accuracy under topic shift. On PRISM it beats baselines for in-distribution users but not held-out users. Summaries also personalize GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 without fine-tuning (72% and 69% win rates). The work addresses output preference only: it does not model temporal drift or interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
closest_overlap: PLUS is the closest outcome_individual counterpart to USIL. It infers a per-user latent z as an editable natural-language summary from sparse interaction history, which could serve as the z_u = g(h) component in USIL's pi_u(a|s,h^u). It uses user-specific evidence (past conversations and preferences) to personalize, but only for reward and response quality.
remaining_question: Can PLUS-style text summaries encode procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer, how much autonomy to take) and condition an interaction policy rather than a reward model? Do they update as a user's preferences drift across sessions, and do they transfer to held-out users, where PLUS lost to BTL/DPL on PRISM (59.7 vs 62.9/65.3)?

summary: Position: personalization should rest on a user-owned, portable, natural-language preference layer shared across AI services.

A 3x3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) crosses LLM agent autonomy (none, full, risk-contingent) with personalization (none, privacy-aware, full) in message-sending scenarios using participants' real personal information. Full personalization raises privacy concern and lowers trust. Risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent hands control back to the user when a GPT-4o detector flags sensitive content, attenuates these effects, and perceived control mediates this. Full autonomy shows no significant effects. Nothing is learned: the policy is fixed, personalization is by prompting, and the study is single-session with two scenarios. It offers empirical grounding for adaptive autonomy and return-of-control design, but not per-user learning.
closest_overlap: Its risk-contingent autonomy has the agent withhold a message and return control to the user when a GPT-4o detector flags sensitive content, and it shows this changes how personalization affects trust and privacy concern, with perceived control as the mediator [interaction_decisions] [key_results]. This is evidence that autonomy and return-of-control policy matter for user perception. However, the policy is fixed and population-level, and personalization is prompt-based.
remaining_question: Can the risk threshold for handing back control be learned per user, using their own sensitivity labels, approvals, and rejections, and does that further raise perceived control and trust beyond the fixed risk-contingent policy? Does it persist over repeated sessions and other contexts?

summary: This ICML 2024 position paper proposes a roadmap to pluralistic alignment. It formalizes three kinds of pluralistic models: Overton (a spectrum of reasonable responses), steerable (conditioned on attributes), and distributional (matching a population distribution). It also formalizes three kinds of benchmarks: multi-objective, trade-off steerable, and jury-pluralistic. A small experiment on GlobalOpinionQA and MPI finds that most post-alignment LLMs have higher Jensen-Shannon distance to human answer distributions and lower entropy than their base models, which the authors treat as initial rather than conclusive evidence. No model is trained, no individual user data is used, and interaction decisions and temporal adaptation are not addressed. It is useful framing for USIL's outcome-side and evaluation discussion.
closest_overlap: Its steerable pluralism, M(x, a) conditioned on an attribute, and its jury-pluralistic benchmark with per-juror reward models resemble a user-conditioned policy. The jury idea also resembles evaluating against individual raters instead of an average. However, the conditioning is on values, groups, or personas and concerns what the model outputs, not how the agent interacts [personalization][what_is_learned].
remaining_question: Can steerable and jury-pluralistic benchmarks be extended from conditioning outputs on value attributes to measuring per-user procedural adaptation, such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, across sessions? And does the finding that alignment reduces distributional pluralism also hold for interaction behaviors, i.e. does RLHF collapse the diversity of interaction styles?
